title: Wagashi
author: Fulani tradition
desc: Milk warmed to fifty or seventy degrees and set with the juice of Calotropis leaves, the curd boiled about twenty minutes before draining.
longDesc: Wagashi is the Fulani cheese of northern Ghana and the coagulant is what makes it extraordinary: not rennet but the juice of Calotropis procera, the apple of Sodom. Fresh milk is filtered and gently heated to between fifty and seventy degrees, the leaf or stem extract is stirred in, and heating continues until coagulation occurs. The curd is then boiled about twenty minutes before draining in a raffia basket or mesh strainer. It is shaped into balls or cakes, sometimes stained red outside with an extract of guinea-corn leaves, and it is usually sliced and fried before eating.
ingredients: Extract of Calotropis procera leaves or stems — the coagulant
// Optional, for the traditional red exterior
// No volumes or extract quantities are published. See the note.
equipment: Raffia or plastic basket, or a mesh strainer
steps: Heat it gently to between 50 and 70 degrees.
Add the extract from Calotropis procera leaves or stems and stir thoroughly.
Continue heating at the same or a slightly higher temperature until coagulation occurs.
// ENDPOINT: coagulation — the curd separating visibly from the whey.
Drain in a raffia or plastic basket, or a mesh strainer.
Shape into balls or rounded cakes.
Optionally stain the outside red with an extract of guinea-corn leaves.
Slice and fry before eating, with pepper.
chefTips: Calotropis procera is the coagulant and it is a plant, not an animal enzyme — which makes wagashi one of the few traditional vegetarian cheeses anywhere.
Fifty to seventy degrees is the documented range before the extract goes in. Too hot and the proteins set badly.
Boil the curd about twenty minutes AFTER coagulation. That is not a European cheesemaking step and it is what gives wagashi its squeaky, frying-stable texture.
The red exterior comes from guinea-corn leaf extract and is cosmetic — it also makes the cheese recognisable in a market.
It is almost always sliced and fried before eating. Fresh wagashi is bland; fried, it is excellent.
Shelf life is short — one study gives three days — which is why it is fried and salted rather than aged.

Sources disagree completely on the coagulant: Calotropis extract in the two traditional accounts, 'plant extract or commercial rennet' in an optimisation study, and plain white vinegar in a modern adaptation. Vinegar will give you a cheese; it will not give you wagashi.
commonMistakes: Using rennet or vinegar and calling it wagashi.
Overheating the milk before adding the extract.
Expecting it to keep — it is a three-day cheese.
sources: PUBLISHED AS A DOCUMENTED PROCESS, NOT A HOUSEHOLD RECIPE. NO VOLUMES, NO EXTRACT QUANTITIES AND NO pH are published in any acceptable source; none have been invented and the ingredient list says so.

PRIMARY SOURCE: Akabanda F., 'A Compilation of the Traditional Processing Techniques and Microbiome in Ghanaian Fermented Milk Products', International Journal of Microbiology and Biotechnology, 2025, Department of Food Science and Technology, University for Development Studies, Tamale. Confirmed across two fetches. Verbatim: 'Fresh milk is first filtered and gently heated to a temperature range of 50-70°C. The extract from C. procera leaves or stems is then added to the warmed milk, stirred thoroughly, and further heated at the same or slightly elevated temperature until coagulation occurs. The curd formed is allowed to boil for about 20 min before draining in a raffia or plastic basket, or mesh strainers'. NOTE: that paper NAMES NO FULANI OR DAGOMBA COMMUNITY; the Fulani attribution comes from the other sources below.

THE OLDEST ACCOUNT, Whitby 1968, 'Foods of Ghana', verbatim: 'The milk is coagulated by adding the juice of Calotropis procera leaves to it, after heating, and is put into a basket for the liquid part to drain off. The curd is then shaped into balls or rounded cakes, sometimes stained red on the outside with an extract of guinea-corn leaves. This "wagashi" will keep for several days or even longer. It is usually cut into slices and fried, and then eaten with the addition of pepper.' That is the source for the red staining and for the frying.

AN OPTIMISATION STUDY whose figures cannot be scaled: Arthur A.B., 'Optimising the Wagashie (A Traditional Cottage Cheese) Process and Sensory Quality', University of Ghana, July 2016. SINGLE-PASS. Traditional process: '23 g of salt, 150 g of plant extract and 0 h fermentation'; improved: '11 g of salt, 5.35ml of commercial rennet and 4 h fermentation'; moisture '(60%)'; 'short shelf life of 3 days', extended to 3 weeks by vacuum packing plus irradiation. THE MILK VOLUME IS NOT PRINTED, so the 23 g and 150 g CANNOT BE SCALED to a batch. That is why no quantities appear above.

A MODERN ADAPTATION, NOT traditional and flagged: Fafa Gilbert, 'Wagashi (The West African Cheese Recipe)', 24 January 2021 — a VINEGAR version: 2.2 litres (4 pints) organic whole milk; 118ml distilled white vinegar; 2 tablespoons salt; 200ml vegetable oil for frying. NO times and NO temperatures; the method is video only. Her useful notes are quoted: "The Fulani's (from the Northern part of Ghana) first introduced Wagashi into Ghana", and traditionally it uses 'pounded leaves of the Apple of Sodom plant and salt'. Her own text therefore identifies her vinegar as the substitution. The Fulani attribution above rests on this note.

THE COAGULANT DISAGREEMENT, unreconciled and material: Calotropis procera extract (Whitby 1968 and Akabanda 2025, with Akabanda giving 50-70°C and a roughly 20-minute curd boil); 'plant extract' OR 'commercial rennet' (Arthur 2016); and distilled white vinegar (Fafa Gilbert). These produce different cheeses and no source reconciles them.
ON THE PLANT: Calotropis procera is the apple of Sodom or Sodom apple, a milkweed whose latex contains proteolytic enzymes. It is the traditional coagulant across the Sahel.

A RELATED PRODUCT from the same 2025 paper, not asked for but recorded: NUNU, the Fulani fermented milk, whose fermentation 'completed within 12 to 24 hours' in the hot season and 'up to 48 hours' in the cold, giving a 'thick, creamy... viscous texture with a white-to-yellowish appearance'. NO pH is given. It is not published here as a separate entry.
DATA FROM BENIN was deliberately not used, being outside Ghana.
storage: 3 days, per the published study. Fry it or salt it heavily to extend that.
healthBenefits: High in complete milk protein and calcium.
Coagulated with a plant enzyme, so suitable for vegetarians.
A significant protein source in pastoral northern diets.
culturalNote: Wagashi is Fulani cheese, made by herding communities across the Sahel and brought into Ghana from the north, and its plant coagulant is a genuinely distinct cheesemaking tradition rather than a variation on a European one. Sliced, fried and dusted with pepper, it is sold at roadsides and is one of the few West African foods with no southern equivalent at all.
